name: Laminectomy

lead: A laminectomy removes the lamina, the bony arch at the back of a vertebra, to widen the spinal canal and take pressure off the spinal cord or nerve roots. It is mainly used for spinal stenosis, tumours, disc problems and some myelopathies. In height and posture discussions it comes up because spine surgery can change how upright and mobile someone is.

The operation is a decompression procedure, not a lengthening one. Large randomized trials have compared laminectomy alone with laminectomy plus fusion for slipped-vertebra stenosis, and reviews describe a rare complication, post-laminectomy kyphosis, in which the spine curves forward after the bone and ligaments that stabilise it are removed.

paras: It is performed by neurosurgeons or orthopaedic spine surgeons under general anaesthesia, through an open or minimally invasive approach, after imaging has confirmed compression. Fusion with screws and rods is sometimes added when the spine is unstable. Recovery involves rehabilitation over weeks to months.

Listed risks include bleeding, infection, blood clots, nerve injury, spinal fluid leak, persistent or returning pain, and post-laminectomy kyphosis or instability, which may need further surgery. It is a medical operation with medical indications, and decisions are made with a spine surgeon.

chain: Removes lamina to decompress cord or nerves
Relieves pain or neurological compression in the spine
May allow more upright, comfortable posture and mobility
angle.text: The procedure is done for medical decompression, and any effect on how tall or upright someone looks comes through relief of symptoms that were forcing a stooped posture. It does not add vertebral length, and post-operative kyphosis is a documented way it can change posture in the other direction.

lead: A laminectomy is a spinal operation in which the surgeon removes the lamina, the rear bony arch of a vertebra, and sometimes adjacent ligament and spinous process, to enlarge the spinal canal and relieve pressure on the spinal cord or nerve roots.[1][2] It is most often performed for spinal stenosis and is also used to reach tumours, to access discs, and to treat some deformities.[2]

In looksmaxxing and height discussions it appears as a spinal procedure whose aftermath can affect posture, since an upright, well-aligned spine contributes to standing height and presentation. The operation itself removes bone from the back of the vertebra and is aimed at neurological relief; it does not lengthen the spine. Relief of nerve compression can allow some patients to stand straighter and walk further, while complications such as kyphosis can do the opposite.[3][4]

Research on laminectomy is extensive: randomized trials compare it with nonsurgical care, with added fusion, and with minimally invasive decompression.[5][6][7] The first laminectomy is attributed to Victor Horsley in 1887.[2]
infobox: Spinal stenosis, tumour, disc herniation, myelopathy
Open, minimally invasive, laminotomy, laminoplasty, with or without fusion

paras: The lamina forms the back wall of the spinal canal. In a laminectomy the surgeon trims or removes it, and in some cases the spinous process and ligament as well, using drills or other bone-removing instruments. Open surgery detaches back muscles to reach the bone, whereas minimally invasive versions use tubular retractors or endoscopes to preserve more muscle. A laminotomy removes only part of one lamina.[2]
A related operation, laminoplasty, opens and rehinges the lamina rather than removing it, and is used in the cervical spine; an open-door technique was reported in 1983.[8]

Severe spinal stenosis is the most common reason, with other uses including relieving cord compression, removing masses, treating deformity and reaching discs during discectomy.[2] Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis with stenosis and degenerative cervical myelopathy are two conditions in which laminectomy-based decompression has been studied and where guidelines address surgical timing.[9][4]

Standing height depends partly on the spine's curvature and alignment. Because laminectomy removes posterior structures that help stabilise the spine, reviews of the cervical operation describe post-laminectomy kyphosis, a forward curvature that is rare but can be serious, and recommend assessing sagittal alignment before surgery.[3] A long-term Japanese follow-up of patients operated for spinal cord tumours reported kyphosis in 27.6% and instability in 24.1% of patients.[10] Surgeons sometimes add fusion where instability is a concern.[2]

The SPORT trial reported by Weinstein and colleagues compared decompressive laminectomy, with or without fusion, with usual nonsurgical care for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis.[11] A 2016 randomized trial compared laminectomy plus fusion with laminectomy alone in stable grade I spondylolisthesis with stenosis.[5] A 2015 pragmatic study compared minimally invasive decompression with open laminectomy for central lumbar stenosis.[6] In cervical myelopathy, a 2021 randomized trial compared ventral with dorsal surgery for patient-reported physical function.[7] A Cochrane review has examined rehabilitation after lumbar disc surgery.[12]

Listed complications are bleeding, infection, blood clots, nerve injury and spinal fluid leak; pain may persist or recur because the operation does not halt degeneration.[2] Post-laminectomy kyphosis and instability are documented structural complications.[3][10] A 1986 case report is titled as a caution about unnecessary laminectomy.[13]
Minimally invasive procedures generally recover faster than open surgery, and adding fusion lengthens recovery to several months or more.[2] Physical therapy is commonly part of rehabilitation.[12]

timeline.event: Victor Horsley performs the first laminectomy.[2]
Expansive open-door laminoplasty for cervical stenotic myelopathy is reported as an alternative that keeps the lamina.[8]
NEJM publishes a trial of surgical versus nonsurgical treatment for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis.[11]
Randomized trial compares laminectomy with and without fusion.[5]
